title: Cleaning as practice
hookLine: Herbert sweeps a room 'as for thy laws'; Baizhang won't eat on a day without work
tomorrow: where does the word saunter come from, if you ask Thoreau?

cards: There's a whole corner of the internet where people film themselves cleaning one messy room, start to finish, and strangers find it calming.
Two old answers say sweeping can be more than a chore, and they don't quite agree.
One is a poem by George Herbert, an English priest and poet, called The Elixir: "Who sweeps a room, as for thy laws, makes that and th' action fine." The other is a story from Chan Buddhism.
Baizhang, an old teacher, worked every day alongside his monks. Worried for him, they hid his tools. He didn't work that day, and he didn't eat either.

teach.h: HERBERT: WHO IT'S FOR CHANGES IT.
teach.b: So: sweep for God, or just sweep? Herbert's side first. The broom is ordinary.
What changes it is who it's for. Done for God, the plainest chore becomes, in his poem, fine, even shining. That's a Christian teaching about vocation: no work is too low to be offered.
Its best case: without a for, chores feel like drudgery, and the for is what turns them into a gift. Now the Zen side.

teach.h: SAMU: THE WORK IS THE PRACTICE.
teach.b: Zen monasteries call daily work samu, work as practice. The point isn't to add a meaning on top. Sweeping is sweeping, done completely, and that's the practice.
Its best case: the moment you sweep for something else, even something holy, part of you has left the broom. Notice what they share.
Neither one rushes the floor to get to the real thing. Neither one splits life into chores and practice.

teach.h: THROUGH THE WORK, OR INTO IT.
teach.b: The honest difference is direction: Herbert points through the work to God; Zen points all the way into the work itself.
This path keeps both on the hook by the door, with their names on.

how: Some Christians offer daily chores to God, as in Herbert's poem; Zen monasteries keep samu, a period of daily work done as practice. People on this path clean one corner slowly, either way.

o: cleaning done slowly, as a practice in itself
a chore chart that splits housework fairly

games.q: your friend says sweeping 'for God' is an add-on: just sweep. what's the best case for Herbert's side?
o: doing it for someone you love turns drudgery into a gift; the 'for' gives it meaning.
Herbert mainly wanted people to clean more, so he made it sound holy.
Herbert held that only a priest's work is holy, so servants should pray instead.
games.why: for Herbert, the plainest chore done for God becomes fine. the Zen side answers that the work is already whole. both refuse to rush the floor.

practice: If there's a cloth or a bit of dust within reach, clean one small corner, a desk, a sill, a shelf, slowly, for the rest of the sit. If you can't move, run your hand slowly along one surface near you.
Do it for someone, as Herbert would, or just do it completely, as a Zen student would.

wordCard.voice: Cleaning as practice: Herbert sweeps as for God's laws; Zen calls daily work samu. Either way, the broom isn't in a hurry.

orig.note: Japanese, from Chinese: work service, Zen's daily work done as practice.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: sweep, for God or simply for the sweeping itself. Five of fourteen, done.
